title: The Tale of an Enum and a BeanPropertyRowMapper: A Spring Developer's Quest
author: Niaz Bin Siraj
excerpt: A real-world debugging story about how Spring's BeanPropertyRowMapper fails with custom enum mappings, and how extending it with a custom RowMapper provides a clean, future-proof solution.
contents:
It was a quiet afternoon in my coding world when a peculiar bug showed up. I was working on a Spring-based web application, mapping database records to Java objects using BeanPropertyRowMapper. Everything seemed routine - until an enum property decided to throw an exception.

The Problem Unveiled

The issue started with a simple class, representing an order in my application:

public class Order {
    private Long id;
    private OrderStatus status;

    // Getters and setters
}

And here was the culprit, the OrderStatus enum:

public enum OrderStatus {
    PENDING(1),
    SHIPPED(2),
    DELIVERED(3),
    CANCELLED(4);

    private final int value;

    OrderStatus(int value) {
        this.value = value;
    }

    public int getValue() {
        return value;
    }
}
warning
The Core Mismatch

The database stored OrderStatus as numeric codes (1, 2, 3, 4), but BeanPropertyRowMapper maps enums using ordinal values by default - meaning it expected 0, 1, 2, 3 instead.

Ordinal vs Custom Value Mapping
DB Value: 1→BeanPropertyRowMapper→Ordinal 1 = SHIPPED (Wrong!)
The mapper interprets the database integer as an ordinal index, not the custom value assigned in the enum constructor.

The Bug That Would Not Budge

I watched in frustration as my application spat out error after error, complaining about mismatched types. The issue was clear: Spring's BeanPropertyRowMapper had no idea how to handle the custom OrderStatus mapping. It was mapping enums based on ordinal values by default, which was not what I needed.

Default Behavior
Ordinal
Maps enum by position index (0, 1, 2, 3). Breaks if enum order changes or DB uses custom codes.
What We Need
Custom Value
Maps enum by its constructor-assigned value (1, 2, 3, 4). Stable and explicit.

For a moment, I thought about hacking the database layer to store enum ordinals. But that idea made my inner developer cringe - what if the enum order changed later? No, the solution had to be clean, reusable, and future-proof.

key
Why Ordinals Are Dangerous

If someone reorders the enum constants or inserts a new value in the middle, every existing database record silently maps to the wrong status. This class of bug is notoriously hard to catch in code review and only surfaces in production.

The Eureka Moment

After diving deep into countless blogs, documentation pages, and forum threads, the solution finally began to take shape: I needed to extend BeanPropertyRowMapper and teach it how to handle enums like OrderStatus.

The first step was to enhance the OrderStatus enum by adding a static fromValue method. This method maps the database-stored numeric codes to the corresponding enum values. Here is how the enum was updated:

public enum OrderStatus {
    PENDING(1),
    SHIPPED(2),
    DELIVERED(3),
    CANCELLED(4);

    private final int value;

    OrderStatus(int value) {
        this.value = value;
    }

    public int getValue() {
        return value;
    }

    public static OrderStatus fromValue(int value) {
        for (OrderStatus status : values()) {
            if (status.value == value) {
                return status;
            }
        }
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown enum value: " + value);
    }
}
lightbulb
The fromValue Pattern

Adding a static factory method like fromValue() to your enums is a widely used pattern in Java. It decouples the database representation from the enum's declaration order, making your code resilient to refactoring.

And here is how I crafted my custom RowMapper:

import org.springframework.jdbc.core.BeanPropertyRowMapper;

import java.beans.PropertyDescriptor;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;

public class OrderRowMapper extends BeanPropertyRowMapper {

    public OrderRowMapper(Class mappedClass) {
        super(mappedClass);
    }

    @Override
    protected Object getColumnValue(ResultSet rs, int index, PropertyDescriptor pd)
            throws SQLException {
        if ("status".equalsIgnoreCase(pd.getName()) && pd.getPropertyType().isEnum()) {
            int statusValue = rs.getInt(index);
            return OrderStatus.fromValue(statusValue);
        }

        return super.getColumnValue(rs, index, pd);
    }
}
How It Works
Custom getColumnValue Override

By overriding the getColumnValue method, we intercept the mapping for the status column specifically. When the property is an enum, we read the raw integer from the ResultSet and use our fromValue() factory method instead of the default ordinal-based mapping.

Custom Mapper Flow
DB Value: 1→OrderRowMapper→fromValue(1)→PENDING (Correct!)
The custom mapper routes enum columns through our fromValue() method, correctly translating database codes to enum constants.

The Test of Courage

Armed with my new OrderRowMapper, I was ready to face the database again. I updated my repository to use the custom mapper:

import org.springframework.jdbc.core.JdbcTemplate;

import java.util.List;

public class OrderRepository {

    private final JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate;

    public OrderRepository(JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate) {
        this.jdbcTemplate = jdbcTemplate;
    }

    public List findAllOrders() {
        String sql = "SELECT id, status FROM orders";
        return jdbcTemplate.query(sql, new OrderRowMapper(Order.class));
    }
}

When I ran the application, everything just worked. The database codes (1, 2, 3, 4) were correctly mapped to their respective OrderStatus values. It felt great - my application finally had the clarity it needed.

Step 1
Add fromValue() to the Enum
Create a static factory method that maps database codes to enum constants, decoupling from ordinal positions.
Step 2
Extend BeanPropertyRowMapper
Override getColumnValue() to intercept enum properties and route them through your factory method.
Step 3
Use the Custom Mapper in Your Repository
Replace the default BeanPropertyRowMapper with your custom OrderRowMapper in JdbcTemplate queries.

Lessons Learned

This little adventure taught me several important lessons:

  1. Do not settle for defaults. While BeanPropertyRowMapper works great out of the box, customizing it for specific use cases can make your application more robust.
  2. Enums are powerful allies. The fromValue method in my enum not only solved this bug but also made the code more expressive and maintainable.
  3. Ordinals are fragile. Never rely on enum ordinal values for persistence. Always use explicit, stable identifiers that do not change when you refactor your code.

Pro Tip

If you have many enums that follow this pattern, consider creating a generic EnumAwareBeanPropertyRowMapper that uses reflection to find a fromValue method on any enum type. This way, you write the mapping logic once and reuse it across your entire application.

Have you faced similar challenges with BeanPropertyRowMapper or enums in your projects? The key takeaway is simple: when the framework's default behavior does not match your domain model, extend it rather than fighting it.
